steps.title: The CA inventory
steps.body: Certification Authorities lists every CA in this instance with its status, type, key and expiry. From here you create a new CA, bring in an existing one, or open one to inspect its certificate and settings.

steps.title: Create a root of trust
steps.body: Create New CA opens a page that groups the options in two blocks: Create (New Key Pair or Reuse Existing Key) and Import (With Private Key or Certificate Only).
steps.note: This example creates a root that issues directly. For an operational hierarchy, see Hierarchy and rotation.

steps.title: New key pair
steps.body: New Key Pair is marked Recommended: a new key pair is generated and fully managed by the KMS, so you do not handle the private key.
steps.note: Which algorithms you can choose depends on what the crypto engine supports.

steps.title: Key algorithm
steps.body: Key Type offers the algorithm families RSA and ECDSA. ECDSA gives shorter keys and signatures than RSA at a comparable security level.

steps.title: Curve: P-384
steps.body: The curve list is labelled P-384 (NIST P-384, secp384r1). P-384 offers roughly a 192-bit security level, above P-256, which makes it a common choice for long-lived roots.
steps.note: Check that the devices and validators that will verify this CA support the curve.

steps.title: CA name = Common Name
steps.body: The CA name becomes the Common Name (CN) of the certificate subject. With CA Type set to Root CA the issuer is Self-signed, so the issuer of the new certificate carries the same name.
steps.note: Name the authority after its purpose, not after a person.

steps.title: Country (C)
steps.body: Optional. Use the two-letter ISO 3166-1 code, here ES. Fill it only if your policy requires it.
steps.note: The subject is part of the signed certificate: changing it later means issuing a new certificate.

steps.title: Organization (O)
steps.body: Optional. The organization or team that operates the CA. It appears in the subject of the CA certificate, which is also its issuer because the root is self-signed.

steps.title: CA validity
steps.body: The field starts with 10y; here it is set to 1y. Accepted units are y, w, d, h, m and s. A CA must outlive the certificates it issues, so plan its validity longer than theirs.
steps.note: 1y is only for this evaluation. A CA created on 17/11/2026 with 1y expired on 16/11/2027 in this recording.

steps.title: Issuance profile
steps.body: The Default Issuance Profile is the profile this CA uses by default when it issues certificates. Client Certificates ("Profile for issuing client certificates") has a validity of 1y1d and the DigitalSignature key usage.
steps.note: This is the profile for the certificates the CA issues, not for the CA's own certificate: that one is the separate CA Certificate Profile section, left on No Profile.

steps.title: Create the authority
steps.body: Lamassu generates the key in the engine and signs the self-signed root certificate. The values you entered are fixed in that certificate once it is signed.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.body: Open the new CA and confirm the ACTIVE status, the issuer C=ES, O=Acme, CN=Acme Showcase Root CA, the validity dates and the ECDSA 384 key.

steps.title: Certificate PEM
steps.body: The Certificate PEM tab shows the public CA certificate as PEM-encoded X.509, with Copy and .pem download buttons, plus the Full Chain bundle.
steps.note: Verify it with OpenSSL: CA:TRUE and a key usage that allows certificate signing (this CA has CertSign and CRLSign). A valid self-signature does not install trust in other systems; distribute the root explicitly.
